title: Staying Ahead of Slovakia's eInvoicing Mandate with SAP Business Network for Procurement
author: yogesh-sap
text:
With Slovakia's structured eInvoicing mandate taking effect on 1 January 2027, businesses have a defined and shrinking window to prepare. SAP Business Network for Procurement is already ready. 
 The Mandate: What's Changing 
 From 1 January 2027, all VAT-registered businesses established in Slovakia must issue, send, and receive structured electronic invoices for domestic B2B and B2G transactions. Governed by Act No. 385/2025, the mandate requires invoices to comply with the EN 16931 European standard, using UBL BIS 3.0 format, and exchanged through Peppol-accredited access points known in Slovakia as certified "Digital Postmen." Invoice data must be reported to Slovakia's Financial Administration in near real time. Invoices must also be archived for 10 years (20 years for real estate transactions). Importantly, intra-EU and cross-border transactions are out of scope until July 2030, when Slovakia aligns with the broader EU VIDA timeline. A PDF sent by email will no longer satisfy legal requirements for domestic transactions. 
 The Challenge for Businesses 
 Complying with the Slovak mandate requires more than updating an invoice template. Businesses must connect to an accredited Peppol access point, register with the Slovak Financial Administration's certified provider registry, and configure both inbound and outbound invoice flows in their systems. For buyers, this means ensuring their ERP and procurement platforms can receive structured UBL BIS 3.0 invoices from external Peppol networks and route them correctly for processing. For suppliers, it means verifying that their invoicing systems or their customers' platforms can generate and validate EN 16931-compliant invoices automatically. Supplier onboarding adds further complexity: every trading partner must also be aligned. With 2026 designated as the transitional preparation year, the window to act is already open. 
 How SAP Business Network for Procurement Helps 
 SAP Business Network for Procurement supports both the inbound and outbound invoice flows required under the Slovak mandate, and the preparation work is already done. 
 For the inbound flow, SAP Document and Reporting Compliance (DRC) Cloud Edition has been officially registered as an accredited "Digital Postman" by Slovak tax authorities and is listed on the Financial Administration's certified provider registry. This means buyers using SAP Business Network can receive Peppol-delivered UBL BIS 3.0 invoices from any Slovak supplier, even those not on the network, with invoices automatically converted to cXML for seamless ERP integration. 
 For the outbound flow, the experience for suppliers remains familiar: the standard PO Flip process is unchanged. Upon invoice issuance, SAP Business Network automatically converts the invoice to UBL BIS 3.0, making it the legal invoice for domestic transactions, and attaches it alongside the cXML. Country and business validations are applied before delivery, helping buyers achieve higher auto-posting rates in their backend systems. 
 The Slovak mandate is already live on SAP Business Network on SAP Business Network on SAP Business AI Platform, with support for current-generation customers arriving in the December 2026 service pack, on time for the mandate. Customers on Commerce Automation or Grow SKUs are entitled to a free SAP DRC license covering up to 10,000 or 50,000 documents per year respectively, reducing the cost of getting connected. Built-in archiving support ensures both buyers and suppliers can meet the mandatory 10-year retention requirement without additional infrastructure. 
 Getting Started 
 2026 is Slovakia's preparation year, and readiness steps like Peppol registration, DRC configuration, and supplier onboarding take time. Whether you are assessing your current setup or ready to begin configuration, SAP Business Network for Procurement provides a clear, accredited path to compliance. To learn more about how SAP Business Network supports eInvoicing compliance in Slovakia and globally, visit the Business Network page or speak with your SAP account team.

title: What I’ve Learned About Customer Concerns Around AI in Procurement
author: Lars_Elmquist
text: Procurement AI: What customers are really worried about — and what's actually changed Procurement teams aren't asking whether AI can do the work. They're asking whether they can trust it with supplier decisions, prove it when something goes wrong, and govern it before it acts on their behalf. This brief synthesises findings from multiple independent research sources into one visual overview — covering the five concerns that surface most consistently, what's genuinely improved in the last six months, what's coming next, and a practical framework for positioning where your customer sits on the path to AI autonomy. Six sections. Grounded in research. Built for conversation.

title: Closing the Gap: SAP Signavio standardizes Audit Events
author: Sanket_Totewar
text:
SAP Signavio audit logs are being updated to align with SAP's evolving standards. If you use multiple SAP products and access audit logs through the ALS Viewer or Search API, this change directly affects you. Here you'll find everything you need to know about what's changing and when, so you can plan ahead and stay ahead. 
 Who Is Affected? 
 This change is primarily relevant for customers who: 
 Use the Audit Log Search API or Audit Log Viewer, AND 
 Have automation, dashboards, alerts, or reports that depend on specific audit event types or event fields that are expected to change 
 What Is Changing? 
 Historically, some SAP Signavio audit information was provided through the zzzCustomEvent event type. To streamline security logs for SAP customers, SAP regularly evaluates the content within custom events and standardizes content across SAP products. To align with these SAP-wide audit logging standards, Signavio is moving information from the zzzCustomEvent to dedicated standardized event types based on the SAP standard audit logging template. The end goal is that the underlying information remains available, but it will no longer be delivered exclusively through zzzCustomEvent. 
 To make the transition easier, SAP has devised a phased approach which will allow customers to adapt to any processes and integrations that may be affected by this change. 
 Transition Timeline 
 To help you update integrations without disruption, SAP introduced a phased transition period. 

 Period 
 Availability 

 From now until December 1, 2026 
 Information is available in both zzzCustomEvent and the new standardized event names 

 After December 1, 2026 
 Information is available only in the new standardized event names 
 This approach is expected to provide you with time to review and update any configurations that rely on the existing event structure. 
 Here is a list of all changes expected in this wave. 

 Event Logged 
 Before 1 Dec 
 After 1 Dec 

 · Process documentation template created 
 · Simulation scenario created 
 · File imported

 · Report exported 
 · File exported

 · Usage of workflow permissions changed 
 · Approval state changed 
 · Approval expiration changed

 · User synchronization started 
 · Configuration synchronization started

 · Approval state created 
 · Approval expiration created

 · Approval expiration deleted

 · Permission assignment created for user

 · Permission assignment created from group

 authnPrivilegeToGroupAdd 

 · Permission assignment deleted for user

 authnPrivilegeToUserDelete 

 · Permission assignment deleted from group

 · User marked for deletion 
 · User license revoked

 · User authentication succeeded

 What Should I Do? 
 If you use the Audit Log Viewer or Search API as part of a process, we recommend that you: 
 Review existing integrations, dashboards, alerts, and monitoring configurations. 
 Identify any dependencies on zzzCustomEvent. 
 Update searches, parsing rules, and downstream systems to use the new standardized event types for data after December 1, 2026. 
 Validate your configuration during the transition period while both event formats are available. 
 Conclusion 
 This change is part of SAP's broader commitment to consistent, unified security logging across its product portfolio. The transition period running until December 1, 2026 gives you a practical window to review, test, and update any configurations at your own pace but acting early means more time to validate while both event formats are still available. If you have questions beyond what's covered below, reach out to SAP Support or consult the related documentation linked at the end of this post. 
 Frequently Asked Questions 
 What happens if I don't update my configuration in time? 
 Any automation that relies exclusively on zzzCustomEvent may stop receiving the expected audit information after December 1, 2026. To avoid interruptions, SAP strongly recommends updating configurations during the transition period when data is available in both formats. 
 Will audit information be lost? 
 No. The information currently available through zzzCustomEvent is being moved to standardized audit event types. The goal is to improve consistency across SAP products while maintaining access to relevant audit information. The information is still available within the retention period of 90 days. 
 Do I need to change anything if I only use the ALS Viewer? 
 In most cases, no action is required. The primary impact is on customers who consume audit logs programmatically through the Search API or external monitoring solutions. You should only be aware of these changes for any post processing done on your security logs. 
 How long are audit logs retained? 
 Audit logs are retained for up to 90 days (three months) from the time they are generated. Customers should refer to the latest SAP Help documentation for current retention information. 
 Where can I learn more? 
 Additional information about SAP Audit Log Service, the ALS Viewer, and the Audit Log Search API is available in SAP Help.

title: Migrate Principal Propagation Configuration from SAP Process Orchestration to SAP Integration Suite
author: ggalves
text: Migrating from PI/PO to SAP Integration Suite raises a frequently underestimated question: how is the logged-in end-user identity propagated from S/4HANA on-premise into Cloud Integration? The legacy Principal Propagation Technical Configuration , built on SSO2 logon tickets, no longer applies, as Cloud Integration authenticates inbound XI calls through XSUAA and OAuth. This article presents a validated end-to-end alternative that carries the user identity over the XI 3.0 protocol by means of an OAuth2 SAML Bearer Assertion flow covering each configuration step, a complete simulation, and a candid assessment of the approach.

title: Charge Calculation based on Agreement for the LTL Process
author: ananth_bhat
text:
For logistics teams running less-than-truckload (LTL) operations, knowing the cost of a shipment shouldn't require a spreadsheet, a carrier call, or a best guess. With the latest update to SAP Logistics Management, agreement-based freight Charge Calculation is now available within the LTL process . 
 SAP Logistics Management is built to simplify logistics execution for businesses with basic to medium complexity warehousing and domestic LTL or parcel shipping needs. The addition of Charge Calculation in the LTL process extends that simplicity to freight cost management — closing one of these steps in the loops in the end-to-end outbound flow.

title: Automating Sales Order Creation from Emails in SAP S/4HANA Cloud Public Edition
author: karen_feng
text:
For many companies, a significant portion of customer purchase orders still arrives by email — as PDF attachments, or plain text in the email body. Sales representatives must manually monitor their inboxes, read each email, and manually enter the order data into the system. This introduces processing delays and data entry errors. 
 SAP S/4HANA Cloud Public Edition addresses this directly with a premium AI feature that turns emailed purchase orders into accurate sales orders — reducing manual effort and accelerating order processing.

title: Who Changed My PO Quantity? Building a Quantity Change Audit Report with Change Documents in ABAP
author: reddysekharpathipati
text:
Introduction 
 SAP records the answer in change documents tables CDHDR and CDPOS. The standard transactions, such as ME23N’s change view and report RSSCD100, show changes one document at a time. They do not give a consolidated, auditable, year-wide view. That view is what internal audit, procurement managers and controllers usually want. 
 In this blog I’ll walk through a small ABAP report, ZPO_QTY_CHANGE_REPORT, that: 
 picks all purchase orders created in a given year 
 reads every quantity EKPO Menge change made to those POs 
 shows old quantity, new quantity and the difference 
 shows who changed it user ID and full name, when, and with which transaction 
 groups the result by the quarter in which the PO was created 
 displays everything in a sortable, filterable ALV grid 
 You can adapt the same pattern to any other field, such as price, delivery date or plant. 
 Business scenario 
 Business question Where the report answers it 

 Which PO items had their quantity changed? PO number, item, description 
 What was the change? Old quantity, new quantity, difference 
 Who made the change and when? User ID, full name, date, time 
 Through which transaction? Transaction code (for example ME22N) 
 In which quarter was the PO created? Quarter (Q1 to Q4) 
 Typical users: 
 internal audit, procurement managers, controllers and support teams investigating quantity disputes with vendors. 
 Technical background 
 Change documents in SAP 
 CDHDR is the change document header. It holds the object class, object ID, change number, user, date, time and transaction code. 
 CDPOS is the change document item. It holds the table name, table key, field name, change indicator, and the old and new values. 
 For purchase orders, the change document object class is EINKBELEG, and the object ID is the PO number. 
 Flow chart: 

 Solution design with small snippets 
 The report works in four steps. 
 Get data. Select POs from EKKO for the chosen year, then read CDHDR for those POs (class EINKBELEG). Next read CDPOS filtered to TABNAME = EKPO, FNAME =MENGE and CHNGIND = U (update). Finally read EKPO for item descriptions. 
 Process data. Link each CDPOS line back to its CDHDR header and decode the TABKEY. Convert the character values to quantities, calculate the difference and derive the quarter. 
 Get full names. Join USR21 with ADRP to turn user IDs into readable names. 
 Display. Show the result with CL_SALV_TABLE. 
 1. Decoding TABKEY 
 CDPOS-TABKEY is a concatenation of client, PO number and item number: * TABKEY = CLIENT(3) + EBELN(10) + EBELP(5)
lv_ebeln = ls_pos-tabkey+3(10).
ls_out-ebelp = ls_pos-tabkey+13(5). 
 T his traces every change line back to an exact PO item. 
 Snippet 2: Converting old and new values 
 VALUE OLD and VALUE NEW are stored as text, and negative values can have a trailing minus sign. A helper form moves the sign to the front before converting: IF lv_txt+lv_len(1) = '-'.
 lv_txt = lv_txt(lv_len).
 CONCATENATE '-' lv_txt INTO lv_txt.
ENDIF. 
 3: Difference and quarter ls_out-diff_value = ls_out-old_value - ls_out-new_value. 
 A positive difference means the quantity was reduced. A negative one means it was increased. The quarter comes from the PO creation month through a simple CASE statement. 
 Performance 
 Every FOR ALL ENTRIES is protected by an emptiness check on the driver table. 
 Results are held in sorted tables with unique keys, so READ TABLE uses binary search. 
 5: ALV 
 CL_SALV_TABLE gives sorting, filtering, Excel export and layout saving with very little code. 
 Selection screen: 

 Complete source code REPORT zpo_qty_change_report.

TABLES: ekko.

*---------------------------------------------------------------------*
* TYPES
*---------------------------------------------------------------------*
TYPES: BEGIN OF ty_out,
 ebeln TYPE ekko-ebeln,
 ebelp TYPE ekpo-ebelp,
 txz01 TYPE ekpo-txz01,
 aedat TYPE ekko-aedat,
 udate TYPE cdhdr-udate,
 utime TYPE cdhdr-utime,
 tcode TYPE cdhdr-tcode,
 old_value TYPE ekpo-menge,
 new_value TYPE ekpo-menge,
 diff_value TYPE ekpo-menge,
 changed_by TYPE cdhdr-username,
 fullname TYPE ad_namtext,
 quarter TYPE char2,
 END OF ty_out.

TYPES: BEGIN OF ty_ekko,
 ebeln TYPE ekko-ebeln,
 aedat TYPE ekko-aedat,
 END OF ty_ekko.

TYPES: BEGIN OF ty_ekpo,
 ebeln TYPE ekpo-ebeln,
 ebelp TYPE ekpo-ebelp,
 txz01 TYPE ekpo-txz01,
 END OF ty_ekpo.

TYPES: BEGIN OF ty_obj,
 objectid TYPE cdhdr-objectid,
 END OF ty_obj.

TYPES: BEGIN OF ty_hdr,
 objectclas TYPE cdhdr-objectclas,
 objectid TYPE cdhdr-objectid,
 changenr TYPE cdhdr-changenr,
 username TYPE cdhdr-username,
 udate TYPE cdhdr-udate,
 utime TYPE cdhdr-utime,
 tcode TYPE cdhdr-tcode,
 END OF ty_hdr.

TYPES: BEGIN OF ty_pos,
 objectclas TYPE cdpos-objectclas,
 objectid TYPE cdpos-objectid,
 changenr TYPE cdpos-changenr,
 tabname TYPE cdpos-tabname,
 tabkey TYPE cdpos-tabkey,
 fname TYPE cdpos-fname,
 chngind TYPE cdpos-chngind,
 value_new TYPE cdpos-value_new,
 value_old TYPE cdpos-value_old,
 END OF ty_pos.

TYPES: BEGIN OF ty_user,
 bname TYPE usr21-bname,
 fullname TYPE ad_namtext,
 END OF ty_user.

*---------------------------------------------------------------------*
* DATA
*---------------------------------------------------------------------*
DATA: gt_out TYPE STANDARD TABLE OF ty_out,
 gt_ekko TYPE SORTED TABLE OF ty_ekko
 WITH UNIQUE KEY ebeln,
 gt_ekpo TYPE SORTED TABLE OF ty_ekpo
 WITH UNIQUE KEY ebeln ebelp,
 gt_hdr TYPE SORTED TABLE OF ty_hdr
 WITH UNIQUE KEY objectclas objectid changenr,
 gt_pos TYPE STANDARD TABLE OF ty_pos,
 gt_users TYPE SORTED TABLE OF ty_user
 WITH UNIQUE KEY bname,
 go_alv TYPE REF TO cl_salv_table.

*---------------------------------------------------------------------*
* SELECTION SCREEN
*---------------------------------------------------------------------*
SELECTION-SCREEN BEGIN OF BLOCK b1 WITH FRAME TITLE TEXT-001.

 PARAMETERS: p_year TYPE numc4 OBLIGATORY DEFAULT sy-datum(4).

 SELECT-OPTIONS: s_ebeln FOR ekko-ebeln.

SELECTION-SCREEN END OF BLOCK b1.

*---------------------------------------------------------------------*
* START
*---------------------------------------------------------------------*
START-OF-SELECTION.

 PERFORM get_data.
 PERFORM process_data.
 PERFORM get_fullname.
 PERFORM display_alv.

*---------------------------------------------------------------------*
* GET DATA
*---------------------------------------------------------------------*
FORM get_data.

 DATA: lv_from TYPE sy-datum,
 lv_to TYPE sy-datum,
 lt_obj TYPE STANDARD TABLE OF ty_obj,
 ls_obj TYPE ty_obj,
 lt_hdr TYPE STANDARD TABLE OF ty_hdr,
 ls_ekko TYPE ty_ekko.

 CLEAR: gt_ekko, gt_ekpo, gt_hdr, gt_pos.

 CONCATENATE p_year '0101' INTO lv_from.
 CONCATENATE p_year '1231' INTO lv_to.

* PO HEADER - POs created in selected year
 SELECT ebeln aedat
 FROM ekko
 INTO TABLE gt_ekko
 WHERE ebeln IN s_ebeln
 AND aedat BETWEEN lv_from AND lv_to.

 IF gt_ekko IS INITIAL.
 RETURN.
 ENDIF.

* Prepare PO object IDs
 LOOP AT gt_ekko INTO ls_ekko.

 CLEAR ls_obj.
 ls_obj-objectid = ls_ekko-ebeln.
 APPEND ls_obj TO lt_obj.

 ENDLOOP.

 SORT lt_obj BY objectid.
 DELETE ADJACENT DUPLICATES FROM lt_obj COMPARING objectid.

* CHANGE DOCUMENT HEADER - USER, DATE, TIME, TCODE
 SELECT objectclas
 objectid
 changenr
 username
 udate
 utime
 tcode
 FROM cdhdr
 INTO TABLE lt_hdr
 FOR ALL ENTRIES IN lt_obj
 WHERE objectclas = 'EINKBELEG'
 AND objectid = lt_obj-objectid.

 IF lt_hdr IS INITIAL.
 RETURN.
 ENDIF.

 SORT lt_hdr BY objectclas objectid changenr.
 gt_hdr = lt_hdr.

* CHANGE DOCUMENT ITEM - OLD AND NEW QUANTITY
 SELECT objectclas
 objectid
 changenr
 tabname
 tabkey
 fname
 chngind
 value_new
 value_old
 FROM cdpos
 INTO TABLE gt_pos
 FOR ALL ENTRIES IN lt_hdr
 WHERE objectclas = lt_hdr-objectclas
 AND objectid = lt_hdr-objectid
 AND changenr = lt_hdr-changenr
 AND tabname = 'EKPO'
 AND fname = 'MENGE'
 AND chngind = 'U'.

 IF gt_pos IS INITIAL.
 RETURN.
 ENDIF.

* PO ITEM DESCRIPTION
 SELECT ebeln
 ebelp
 txz01
 FROM ekpo
 INTO TABLE gt_ekpo
 FOR ALL ENTRIES IN gt_ekko
 WHERE ebeln = gt_ekko-ebeln.

ENDFORM.

*---------------------------------------------------------------------*
* PROCESS DATA
*---------------------------------------------------------------------*
FORM process_data.

 DATA: ls_pos TYPE ty_pos,
 ls_hdr TYPE ty_hdr,
 ls_ekko TYPE ty_ekko,
 ls_ekpo TYPE ty_ekpo,
 ls_out TYPE ty_out,
 lv_ebeln TYPE ekko-ebeln,
 lv_month TYPE n LENGTH 2.

 CLEAR gt_out.

 LOOP AT gt_pos INTO ls_pos.

 CLEAR: ls_out, ls_hdr, ls_ekko, ls_ekpo.

* Read change document header
 READ TABLE gt_hdr INTO ls_hdr
 WITH TABLE KEY
 objectclas = ls_pos-objectclas
 objectid = ls_pos-objectid
 changenr = ls_pos-changenr.

 IF sy-subrc <> 0.
 CONTINUE.
 ENDIF.

* TABKEY = CLIENT(3) + EBELN(10) + EBELP(5)
 lv_ebeln = ls_pos-tabkey+3(10).

 ls_out-ebeln = lv_ebeln.
 ls_out-ebelp = ls_pos-tabkey+13(5).

* PO HEADER
 READ TABLE gt_ekko INTO ls_ekko
 WITH TABLE KEY ebeln = lv_ebeln.

 IF sy-subrc <> 0.
 CONTINUE.
 ENDIF.

 ls_out-aedat = ls_ekko-aedat.

* PO ITEM DESCRIPTION
 READ TABLE gt_ekpo INTO ls_ekpo
 WITH TABLE KEY
 ebeln = lv_ebeln
 ebelp = ls_out-ebelp.

 IF sy-subrc = 0.
 ls_out-txz01 = ls_ekpo-txz01.
 ENDIF.

* CHANGE USER DETAILS
 ls_out-udate = ls_hdr-udate.
 ls_out-utime = ls_hdr-utime.
 ls_out-tcode = ls_hdr-tcode.
 ls_out-changed_by = ls_hdr-username.

* OLD AND NEW QUANTITY
 PERFORM conv_qty USING ls_pos-value_old
 CHANGING ls_out-old_value.

 PERFORM conv_qty USING ls_pos-value_new
 CHANGING ls_out-new_value.

* DIFFERENCE
 ls_out-diff_value = ls_out-old_value - ls_out-new_value.

* QUARTER BASED ON PO CREATED DATE
 lv_month = ls_out-aedat+4(2).

 CASE lv_month.
 WHEN '01' OR '02' OR '03'.
 ls_out-quarter = 'Q1'.

 WHEN '04' OR '05' OR '06'.
 ls_out-quarter = 'Q2'.

 WHEN '07' OR '08' OR '09'.
 ls_out-quarter = 'Q3'.

 WHEN '10' OR '11' OR '12'.
 ls_out-quarter = 'Q4'.
 ENDCASE.

* APPEND OUTPUT
 APPEND ls_out TO gt_out.

 ENDLOOP.

 SORT gt_out BY ebeln ebelp udate utime.

ENDFORM.

*---------------------------------------------------------------------*
* CONVERT CHANGE DOCUMENT QUANTITY
*---------------------------------------------------------------------*
FORM conv_qty USING iv_char TYPE cdpos-value_old
 CHANGING cv_qty TYPE ekpo-menge.

 DATA: lv_txt TYPE c LENGTH 30,
 lv_len TYPE i.

 CLEAR cv_qty.

 lv_txt = iv_char.
 CONDENSE lv_txt.

 lv_len = strlen( lv_txt ).

 IF lv_len = 0.
 RETURN.
 ENDIF.

* Trailing minus to leading minus
 lv_len = lv_len - 1.

 IF lv_txt+lv_len(1) = '-'.

 lv_txt = lv_txt(lv_len).

 CONCATENATE '-' lv_txt INTO lv_txt.

 ENDIF.

 TRY.

 cv_qty = lv_txt.

 CATCH cx_sy_conversion_error.

 CLEAR cv_qty.

 ENDTRY.

ENDFORM.

*---------------------------------------------------------------------*
* GET USER FULL NAME
*---------------------------------------------------------------------*
FORM get_fullname.

 DATA: lt_names TYPE STANDARD TABLE OF ty_user,
 ls_user TYPE ty_user.

 FIELD-SYMBOLS: <fs> TYPE ty_out.

 CHECK gt_out IS NOT INITIAL.

 SELECT u~bname,
 a~name_text AS fullname
 FROM usr21 AS u
 INNER JOIN adrp AS a
 ON a~persnumber = u~persnumber
 INTO TABLE @LT _names
 FOR ALL ENTRIES IN @gt_out
 WHERE u~bname = @gt_out-changed_by
 AND a~date_from = '00010101'
 AND a~nation = @Space .

 SORT lt_names BY bname.

 DELETE ADJACENT DUPLICATES FROM lt_names
 COMPARING bname.

 gt_users = lt_names.

 LOOP AT gt_out ASSIGNING <fs>.

 READ TABLE gt_users INTO ls_user WITH TABLE KEY bname = <fs>-changed_by.

 IF sy-subrc = 0.
 <fs>-fullname = ls_user-fullname.
 ENDIF.

 ENDLOOP.

ENDFORM.

title: Como incluir IS, CBS e IBS na base do ICMS sem necessidade de desenvolvimentos?
author: ThalesMacedo
text:
Olá, pessoal, 
 Como venho sendo muito acionado por muitos clientes e amigos, para termos uma 2° carta na manga enquanto aguardamos as SAP notes relacionadas à inclusão dos impostos novos na base do ICMS, gostaria de compartilhar com vocês uma solução que venho compartilhando de fazer esses ajustes sem nenhum desenvolvimento. 
 Pontos importantes: essa solução é para processos de SD, baseada na RVABRA , e precisa ser adaptada à realidade de seu cliente. 
 Segue abaixo o passo-a-passo: 
 Step 1: Criar condições extras (custom) 
 a - Para os novos impostos. 

 b - Para ter o valor do produto (vProd) 

 c - Offset dos novos impostos (única, sumarizando todos os impostos). 

 Step 2: Atualizar os esquemas de cálculos. 

 Step 3: Alterar o mapping de condições para NF-e. 

 Efetuando esses ajustes, os pontos abaixo serão resolvidos: 
 1 – Inclusão dos impostos IS, CBS e IBS na base de cálculo do ICMS. 
 2 – Valor da receita com o valor do vProd, sendo assim os novos impostos não farão parte do valor da receita. 
 3 – Valor do vProd da NF-e sendo mapeado corretamente, sem os valores de IS, CBS e IBS. 
 Obrigado, 
 Thales Macedo

title: Zero Trust in SAP: Why Identity is the New Perimeter in a Hybrid SAP Landscape
author: karthikj2
text:
What SAP's " never trust, always verify" security model means for your landscape and your organization. 
 Zero Trust in SAP: Identity is the New Perimeter 
 The SAP system at the heart of your business holds finance, supply chain, HR and customer data. It is also reachable from more places than ever: cloud apps on SAP BTP, remote employees, partners, APIs and hybrid landscapes that stretch across data centres and hyperscalers. 
 Zero Trust is the strong defense, and SAP aligns its security portfolio to it. 
 What Zero Trust really means 
 Zero Trust is a security model built on one rule: never trust, always verify. 
 It assumes threats exist both inside and outside the traditional network perimeter, so no user, device or system is trusted by default. 
 The three Zero Trust pillars in an SAP context 
 Three pillars carry the model: 
 Verify Explicitly: Authenticate and authorize every request using all available signals: identity, location and device health. 
 Least Privilege Access: Grant only the permissions a person needs. In SAP this is enforced through SAP GRC Access Control, SAP Cloud Identity Access Governance (IAG) and Role Based Access (RBAC) 
 Assume Breach: Design systems expecting that compromise will happen. Monitor continuously and segment access so one incident stays contained. 
 How SAP puts Zero Trust into practice 
 SAP Zero Trust solution map, from identity to monitoring 
 Zero Trust is not one product. It is an architecture built from several SAP capabilities working together: 
 Identity and Access Governance: SAP Cloud Identity Access Governance (IAG) manages access requests, access analysis and role assignments, with continuous compliance checks. 
 SAP GRC Access Control: Enforces segregation of duties (SoD), risk analysis and firefighter-style emergency access controls. 
 Single Sign-On and SAP Cloud Identity Services: Centralised authentication with multi-factor authentication, which cuts the risk of credential-based attacks. 
 SAP BTP Security: OAuth 2.0 and OpenID Connect (OIDC) authentication for cloud-native applications. 
 Network Segmentation: SAP landscape zones (DMZ, internal and cloud) aligned to a Zero Trust architecture. 
 Continuous Monitoring: SAP Enterprise Threat Detection (ETD) brings behavioural analytics and anomaly detection to the SAP application layer. 
 Four concepts every SAP Security professional should know 
 No implicit trust, even for internal users: Employees inside the network are continuously re-verified, not waved through. 
 Micro-segmentation: Isolate SAP systems such as ERP, S/4HANA and BTP so an intruder cannot move laterally. 
 Just-in-time and just-enough access. Elevated rights are temporary and tightly scoped, delivered through SAP GRC - Emergency Access Management / SAP IAG – Privileged Access Management. 
 Device posture validation: Endpoints must be compliant before they are allowed to reach SAP. 
 Built on Open Standards 
 SAP aligns its security portfolio with Zero Trust frameworks such as NIST SP 800-207. It integrates with enterprise identity providers including Microsoft Entra ID, Okta and SAP Cloud Identity Services, so the same policies apply across hybrid landscapes. 
 The takeaway: identity is the new perimeter. Access is granted on verified identity, context and risk, not on network location. 
 What this means for SAP Security Consultant / Architect 
 Zero Trust turns SAP Security Consultant to an Architect who make it work sit across Identity, Governance, Cloud and Application Security operations, and the best candidates combine technological depth with Architectural thinking. 
 SAP Zero Trust talent map, roles mapped to skills 
 Roles / Team to enforce Zero Trust 
 SAP Security and Authorizations Consultant: Role design, least-privilege models and S/4HANA authorization concepts. 
 SAP GRC and IAG Specialist: Access Control, SoD rule sets, risk analysis and emergency access management. 
 SAP Identity and Access Management Engineer: SAP Cloud Identity Services, SSO, MFA and integration with Microsoft Entra ID or Okta. 
 SAP BTP Security Architect. OAuth 2.0, OIDC, secure integration and cloud-native application security. 
 SAP Security Operations Analyst. SAP Enterprise Threat Detection, log analysis and anomaly investigation. 
 SAP Landscape and Network Architect: Zone design, micro-segmentation and hybrid connectivity. 
 Key Takeaway 
 In a Zero Trust world, trust is never assumed. It is earned on every request, based on who is asking, from where, on what device and at what level of risk. 
 For SAP landscapes that span on-premise systems, S/4HANA and SAP BTP, this means treating identity as the new perimeter: verify explicitly, grant least privilege, and always assume breach. Organizations that build these principles into their SAP Architecture today will be better prepared as their landscapes continue to move to the Cloud - Private / Public.

title: SAP Named a Leader in Two 2026 IDC MarketScapes: Worldwide Warehouse Management for Manufacturing and for Retail
author: Till Dengel
text:
SAP has been named a Leader in both the 2026 IDC MarketScape for Worldwide Warehouse Management for Manufacturing* and the 2026 IDC MarketScape for Worldwide Warehouse Management for Retail**. We believe this recognition reflects SAP’s continued focus on helping companies run increasingly complex warehouse operations while connecting logistics more closely with the rest of the business. 

 Warehouse operations are being reshaped by rising fulfillment expectations, labor constraints, automation, and AI. At the same time, warehouses need to coordinate with a growing number of processes and systems beyond their four walls. 

 The requirements can look very different depending on the industry. Manufacturers need to synchronize warehouse operations with production, material availability, quality processes, and automated equipment. Retailers need to manage inventory and fulfillment across stores, distribution centers, e-commerce, and other channels, often while navigating dramatic changes in volume during peak periods. 

 Modern warehouse management needs to bring these pieces together. 
 Keep pace with demand, minimize costs, and maintain sustainable, risk-resilient warehouse operations 

 Learn how 

 Connecting warehouse operations across the business 

 Modelling end-to-end workflows has long been central to our approach to warehouse management at SAP. SAP Extended Warehouse Management (SAP EWM) helps companies manage high-volume warehouse operations while connecting warehousing with processes across production, transportation, quality management, and the broader SAP S/4HANA environment. 

 For manufacturing, this can include staging materials for production, just-in-time and just-in-sequence supply, managing quality-controlled inventory, and tracking batches and serial numbers. SAP EWM also supports integration with warehouse automation, helping companies coordinate inventory and warehouse tasks with conveyors, sorters, automated storage and retrieval systems, and other equipment. 

 Retail brings a different set of demands. SAP EWM can support retail and omnichannel warehouse operations and connect with SAP S/4HANA Retail , SAP Commerce Cloud , and order management capabilities. SAP also offers SAP Logistics Management for companies looking to address less complex warehouse operations. 

 Together, these capabilities can give companies flexibility to support different warehouse requirements while helping to keep logistics connected with the processes that surround it. 

 Mondelēz Australia shows what this can look like at scale . At its new 47,000-square-meter Melbourne distribution center, SAP EWM integrates with an automated storage and retrieval system that orchestrates more than 56,000 pallets in automated storage, while the operation maintains more than 95% on-time, in-full delivery performance. 

 “The collaborative partnership enabled Mondelēz to realize the full potential of SAP’s warehouse and supply chain capabilities,” said Anna Reid, director, Customer Service & Logistics, Mondelēz Australia. 

 Bringing more intelligence into the warehouse 

 AI is adding another dimension to warehouse management. Warehouses create enormous amounts of operational data. The opportunity is to use that data to help teams understand what is happening, anticipate what is likely to happen next, and take action more efficiently. 

 SAP continues to bring AI into warehouse operations in practical ways. Predictive capabilities can support areas such as product slotting and labor planning, while analytics and simulation can help companies identify opportunities to improve warehouse processes. SAP EWM also integrates with SAP Signavio Process Intelligence to help organizations analyze process performance and identify inefficiencies. 

 We are building on that foundation with Joule and agentic AI. Agents can help warehouse teams address routine tasks and exceptions with less manual coordination, connecting decisions with relevant business data and processes. 

 SAP’s WMS solutions already can deliver a broad set of generative AI and AI-assisted predictive capabilities, along with agentic AI capabilities available to customers today, backed by a robust roadmap of AI innovations designed to help keep customers at the forefront of warehouse innovation. 

 SAP is also bringing AI into the physical world. With physical AI , SAP is working to connect business processes and context with robots and other physical systems. In warehouse scenarios, this can enable tasks from SAP EWM to help drive physical execution and return operational results back into SAP, working to create a closed loop between enterprise decisions and warehouse operations. 

 As AI and automation take on a greater role in the warehouse, people remain central to operations. Trust and governance are essential, with people continuing to provide oversight and control while these technologies help warehouse teams reduce manual work, improve productivity, and respond more quickly to changing conditions. 

 Delivering value across warehouse operations 

 Warehouse management continues to evolve as companies connect operations more closely with production, transportation, and fulfillment while introducing new levels of automation and intelligence. 

 We believe the opportunity is to bring these capabilities together in ways that deliver practical results. That means helping companies move goods more efficiently, make better use of people and assets, maintain visibility and control over inventory, and adapt warehouse operations as business needs change. 

 We are proud to be recognized as a Leader in both of these IDC MarketScape vendor assessments. We believe the recognition reinforces the direction we are taking with SAP Extended Warehouse Management and SAP Logistics Management, and we will continue working with our customers to turn innovation into better warehouse operations and business outcomes. 

 Till Dengel is global head of Product Marketing for Logistics and Asset & Service Management at SAP.

title: Successful SAP Transformation Starts With Business Processes, Not Tech
author: Tim Clark
text:
As enterprises embrace AI and modernize their SAP systems, a new book suggests that connecting business processes, architecture, data, and human decision-making is key to successful transformation. 
 SAP BTP: Powering applications, data, and AI to move business forward 

 Learn how 

 Enterprise transformation has never suffered from a shortage of technology. Businesses the world over have spent decades investing in new applications, modernizing infrastructure, and implementing systems designed to make business operations faster, smarter, and more efficient. 

 However, connecting those investments to measurable business outcomes remains an ongoing challenge. As artificial intelligence introduces daily innovations and opportunities for automation and decision-making, the stakes couldn’t be higher. 

 For Kumar Piraviperumal, semiconductor industry leader in the IBM HiTech practice, addressing these challenges begins not with technology, but with understanding how a business actually operates. “My belief is process is the base of all transformation,” he said during a recent SAP PRESS book launch webcast. 

 That primary belief is central to his new book, Integrating Architecture, Processes, and AI on SAP BTP , which explores how organizations can connect business processes, enterprise architecture, data, AI, and employee adoption into meaningful transformation. 

 Instead of categorizing these capabilities as separate technology initiatives, Piraviperumal believes organizations need a connected foundation that carries business intent from process design through application development, deployment, and ongoing governance. 

 Turning transformation theory into practice 

 Piraviperumal’s book is based on an experience he had working on a transformation program for an $8 billion media company operating across 47 countries. 

 The organization ran complex business processes, and his team was among the early adopters attempting to connect SAP Signavio for process modeling with SAP LeanIX for enterprise architecture. 

 The work proved challenging. As the team encountered integration problems, missing information, and inconsistent approaches, Piraviperumal documented what worked, what failed, and how to standardize the process. 

 “The motivation was basically trying to create a practical book for everybody,” he explained. 

 The end result is a guide intended for practitioners who need to translate business requirements into functioning enterprise applications. 

 Its central theme is that transformation requires more than documentation or architectural diagrams. Organizations must create continuity between the processes, systems and the people responsible for using them. 

 Connecting the enterprise from end to end 

 Piraviperumal believes enterprise transformation is a progression that begins with business strategy and extends through value streams, capabilities, processes, resources, data, and technology in the following ways: 

 SAP Signavio provides the process foundation, enabling organizations to analyze how work is performed and identify opportunities for improvement using operational data. 

 SAP LeanIX connects those processes to the underlying application architecture, while SAP Business Technology Platform (SAP BTP) provides capabilities for integration, development, and AI-enabled execution. 

 WalkMe adds another critical dimension: helping employees adopt new processes and applications. 

 This begs the question: How do you make these different technologies work together without losing the connections between business requirements and technical execution? 

 One method is through identifiers. A process modeled in SAP Signavio may have a different identifier in SAP LeanIX and another in WalkMe, making it difficult to maintain a consistent view across systems. 

 Piraviperumal’s team created identifier consistency by creating a common data structure that maps identifiers and connects them to the applications being developed. 

 This “canonical data spine” strategy establishes traceability across the transformation life cycle, which becomes extremely valuable when something goes wrong. 

 A defect in a business application, for example, might originate in the software itself, the original process design, or a business process that has become outdated. Properly managing those connections helps organizations identify the source of a problem rather than treating every issue as an isolated technical failure. 

 “Traceability is one thing which I keep stressing in this book,” said Piraviperumal. 

 Employee adoption before deployment 

 Piraviperumal emphasizes that organizations should consider how employees will interact with new systems before development begins, rather than treating change management as a final implementation activity. 

 His book underscores the importance of digital adoption concepts before moving into the technical build. 

 Using WalkMe, organizations can connect employee guidance and adoption information to the business processes being transformed. The objective is to understand how new workflows will affect employees, anticipate friction, and improve the likelihood that technology investments deliver their intended value. 

 “Business is not interested in SAP,” said Piraviperumal. “They are interested in outcomes.” 

 From process models to AI-generated applications 

 One of the book’s most practical themes is the opportunity to use existing business process models as inputs for AI-assisted application development. 

 During the webcast, Piraviperumal demonstrated how a process designed in SAP Signavio could help generate an application for SAP Analytics Cloud, using a financial close-to-rolling-forecast process. 

 By exporting the approved process model and combining it with architectural information from SAP LeanIX, his team used AI capabilities to identify process issues, generate configuration information, and produce code supporting application development. 

 The demonstration also incorporated IBM watsonx and other tools developed by Cognitus. 

 Instead of relying on an open-ended natural language prompt, the approach instead relies on an existing business process model as the foundation for generating the application. This strategy gives developers a structured starting point while preserving connections to the original business requirements. 

 It also illustrates how AI reduces manual effort involved in translating process documentation into functional specifications, technical configurations, and executable applications. 

 However, Piraviperumal stressed that AI-assisted development does not eliminate the need for developers, configurators, or business validation. 

 Keeping humans in control of AI 

 For all of the cautionary attention surrounding autonomous AI, Piraviperumal believes governance and human oversight remain essential. 

 His transformation framework recognizes three broad constraints: economics, technology, and social adoption. Even when a solution is technically feasible, organizations must consider its cost and whether employees will accept it. 

 AI adds another layer of complexity because automated systems must operate within clearly defined boundaries. 

 Piraviperumal dedicates the book’s final chapters to operational governance, security controls, and audit requirements, arguing that these capabilities are fundamental to trustworthy deployment. 

 He also describes incorporating human validation checkpoints into the code examples included in the book. 

 “AI can only do so much,” he said. “AI cannot make decisions. It can help you with options to make a decision but not on decisions itself.” 

 A more connected future for enterprise transformation 

 The book’s broader message underscores the importance of successful transformation and how it depends on preserving the relationship between business intent and technology execution. 

 Process modeling, enterprise architecture, application development, AI, and employee adoption cannot operate effectively as disconnected disciplines. It must support a continuous, governed system that enables organizations to understand what they are changing, why they are changing it, and whether the results deliver value. 

 For practitioners, the opportunity is to use that connected foundation to make enterprise transformation more repeatable, traceable, and responsive to changing business needs. 

 And even as AI becomes more capable of generating applications and supporting business decisions, Piraviperumal sees human judgment as an enduring part of that equation. 

 “Always remember that human control is still important even in this AI world,” he said.
